title: Vue in an hour
summary: You can read a Vue component and explain what it does: reactivity, templates, props and events, composables, and how Vue works with Laravel.

blocks.text: A Vue app is built from components. A component lives in one file with the extension `.vue`, called a single-file component (SFC). Logic, markup and optionally styles sit together in it.
The blocks of a component

items: `<script setup>`: the logic, in JavaScript or TypeScript. What you declare at the top level can be used directly in the template.
`<template>`: the markup, HTML with Vue syntax mixed in.
`<style>`: CSS for this component. With `scoped` the styles apply only here. You do not always need this block.

blocks.text: A build tool such as Vite compiles each `.vue` file into plain JavaScript and CSS. That is why you can write things in a `.vue` file that a browser does not understand by itself.
Example: a counter

blocks.caption: Counter.vue
blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';

const count = ref(0);

function add(): void {
    count.value++;
}
</script>

<template>
    <button type="button" @click="add">Clicked: {{ count }}</button>
</template>

items: `ref(0)` creates a reactive value with starting value 0. In the script you read and write `count.value`.
In the template you write `{{ count }}`, without `.value`. Vue unwraps the ref there for you.
`@click="add"` calls the function `add` on a click. When `count` changes, Vue redraws the button.

blocks.text: In Sprintlab's own code
`resources/js/components/StatusChip.vue` is a small component that shows a status label. You can see the same parts, here without a `<style>` block.

blocks.caption: StatusChip.vue

items: `defineProps<{ status: TicketStatus; label: string }>()` says which data the parent has to pass in. Lesson 4 covers this.
`tone` is a `computed` that picks the right colour classes from `status`.
In the template, `:class="tone"` sits next to a fixed `class`. Vue merges the two.

blocks.label: What you already know from Laravel
blocks.text: An SFC is like a Blade component: the view and the data it needs belong together. A prop is like an attribute on `<x-alert>`.

blocks.label: As in React
blocks.text: A component here is not a function that returns JSX. The markup sits in a separate `<template>`, and `<script setup>` runs once per component, not on every render.

blocks.label: Say it like this in an interview
blocks.text: A Vue component is a `.vue` file with a script, a template and optional styles. The template can use whatever `<script setup>` declares.

check.question: Why do you write `count.value` in the script but `{{ count }}` in the template?
check.answer: A `ref` is an object with a `.value`. In the script you have to reach for it yourself. In the template, Vue unwraps top-level refs automatically.

deeper.text: Think of a small box with a note inside. The box is the `ref`, the note is the value.
In the script you open the box yourself: `count.value`. In the template Vue does that for you, so you just write `count`.
A component is then a card with three boxes: what it knows (script), what it looks like (template) and which colours it wears (style).

blocks.text: Vue keeps track of which values the template uses. When such a value changes, Vue updates only that part of the page. You work with two tools: `ref` for your own data and `computed` for derived data.
ref and computed

items: `ref(value)`: a reactive value. You read and write `.value` in the script. It can be a number, text or an object.
`computed(() => ...)`: a value Vue calculates from other reactive values. You also read it through `.value`.
A `computed` is cached. Vue only recalculates it when a value it uses changes.
A `computed` should only calculate. It should not change anything else or send requests.

blocks.text: Example: a message box with a counter

blocks.caption: Composer.vue

items: `body` is a `ref` holding the text. `v-model="body"` keeps the field and the ref in sync, in both directions.
`length` and `canSend` are `computed`. You never store or update them yourself; they follow `body` automatically.
`:disabled="!canSend"` disables the button while the message is empty or too long.

blocks.text: In Sprintlab's own code

`resources/js/components/chat/ChatComposer.vue` does the same, only bigger. Here are the data and the three computed values `length`, `canSubmit` and `showCounter`. The snippet is cut down to that part of `<script setup>`.

blocks.caption: ChatComposer.vue (shortened)

items: `length` is the length of the message. `canSubmit` is true when nothing is being sent, the message is not empty and it is not too long.
`showCounter` shows the counter only at 80% of the maximum.
`length.value` needs `.value` because we are in the script. `form.body` does not, because `form` is not a ref but an object with fields.

blocks.label: What you already know from Laravel
blocks.text: A `computed` is like an accessor on an Eloquent model: you read it like a field, but it is calculated from other fields.

blocks.label: As in React
blocks.text: `ref` is like `useState`, but you change it directly with `count.value++`. There is no setter. A `computed` is like `useMemo`, but Vue sees by itself which values it uses. You do not write a dependency array.

blocks.label: Say it like this in an interview
blocks.text: A `ref` holds reactive state, and a `computed` is a cached, derived value that is recalculated when its sources change.

check.question: In `Composer.vue` someone types a character into the field. Which values change, and who takes care of that?
check.answer: `body` changes through `v-model`. Because of that, Vue recalculates `length` and `canSend` and updates the counter and the button. You write no code for it.

deeper.text: A spreadsheet has cells with numbers and cells with a formula. The `ref` is a cell where you type something yourself.
The `computed` is the cell with the formula, for example `=A1+A2`. Change A1 and the result is right again at once. You never edit that cell yourself.

blocks.text: In a `<template>` you write plain HTML, extended with a few special characters and `v-` attributes. These are called directives. Once you know them, you can read almost any Vue template.

rows: Binds an attribute to an expression (short for `v-bind`)
Repeats an element for each item in a list
Keeps an input and a ref in sync, in both directions
Sets classes based on a value

blocks.text: A mustache `{{ }}` works only between tags, as text. In an attribute you use `:`, so `:id="id"` and not `id="{{ id }}"`. A `:` expression is plain JavaScript.
Example: a list

blocks.caption: List.vue

items: `v-if` and `v-else` belong together: the list appears only when there are tickets, otherwise the text. `v-else` comes right after the element with `v-if`.
`v-for` creates one `<li>` per ticket. `:key="ticket.id"` gives each element a stable identity, so Vue recognises the right element when the list changes.
`:class="{ done: ticket.status === 'done' }"` adds the class `done` only when the condition is true.

blocks.text: In Sprintlab's own code
`resources/js/pages/Board.vue` uses the same syntax. First `v-if` and `v-else-if` for two messages.

blocks.caption: Board.vue
blocks.code: Tickets appear here when your first sprint starts. Go to the overview

blocks.text: Then the columns. Note the `v-for` with `:key`, the bound `:class` and `@dragover.prevent`.

blocks.caption: Board.vue
blocks.code:
<section
    v-for="column in columns"
    :key="column.value"
    class="flex min-h-48 flex-col rounded-md border bg-card"
    :class="
        dropTarget === column.value
            ? 'border-primary'
            : 'border-border'
    "
    @dragover.prevent="dropTarget = column.value"
    @dragleave="
        (e: DragEvent) =>
            !(e.currentTarget as HTMLElement).contains(
                e.relatedTarget as Node,
            ) && (dropTarget = null)
    "
    @drop.prevent="onDrop(column.value)"
>

blocks.text: Inside the column are the title with a count and a message when the column is empty.

blocks.caption: Board.vue
blocks.code:
{{ column.label }} {{ column.tickets.length }}

No tickets in {{ column.label.toLowerCase() }}.

blocks.label: What you already know from Laravel
blocks.text: Blade translation: `{{ }}` is `{{ }}`, `v-if` is `@if`, `v-for` is `@foreach`. The difference is that Vue updates the page when the data changes. Blade renders once on the server.

blocks.label: As in React
blocks.text: You write `:class` instead of `className`, `v-if` instead of `&&` or a ternary, and `v-for` with `:key` instead of `.map()` with `key`. The idea of the key is the same.

blocks.label: Say it like this in an interview
blocks.text: In a Vue template, `{{ }}` shows text, `:` and `@` bind attributes and events, and `v-if` and `v-for` control what is rendered.

check.question: Why does `v-for` always get a `:key`, and which value do you pick for it?
check.answer: The key lets Vue recognise each element when the list changes. Pick something unique and stable, such as the item's `id`, and not its position in the list.

deeper.text: The template is a letter with blanks. `{{ }}` is a blank for text. `v-if` is a paragraph you cross out or keep.
`v-for` is a rubber stamp: you press the same line once per item. The `:key` is the number on each print, so with a new batch you know which print belongs to which item.
`:` says 'this is not text but an expression'. `@` says 'do this when that happens'.

blocks.text: Components work together by one rule. Data goes from parent to child as **props**. Messages go from child to parent as **events**.

items: A child declares its props with `defineProps` and its events with `defineEmits`.
A child does not change a prop. The prop is read-only, and Vue warns you if you try.
If the child wants something changed, it sends an event. The parent decides and changes its own data.

blocks.text: Example: a row and its parent

blocks.caption: TicketRow.vue (the child)

items: `defineProps<{ title: string; done: boolean }>()` says which two props the row expects, and their types.
`defineEmits<{ toggle: [] }>()` says the row can send a `toggle` event, with no data.
When the checkbox changes, the row calls `emit('toggle')`. The row does not change `done` itself.

blocks.caption: Parent.vue (the parent)

items: The parent owns the data: the `ref` with tickets.
`:title` and `:done` pass props. `@toggle="toggle(ticket.id)"` listens for the event.
The `toggle` function changes `done` in the parent. The new prop then flows down to the child again.

blocks.text: In Sprintlab's own code
On Sprintlab's board, `Board.vue` shows each ticket with a `TicketCard`. This is how that usage looks in the file, without the two drag events.

blocks.caption: Board.vue (shortened)
blocks.code:
<TicketCard
    v-for="ticket in column.tickets"
    :key="ticket.id"
    :ticket="ticket"
    :statuses="statuses"
    :locked="paused"
    :first="ticket.id === firstTicketId"
    @open="selectedId = ticket.id"
    @move="(status) => move(ticket, status)"
/>

blocks.text: `TicketCard.vue` declares its side of the contract like this.

blocks.caption: TicketCard.vue

items: `:ticket`, `:statuses`, `:locked` and `:first` are props. `first` has a question mark, so it is optional.
`@open` and `@move` are events. `move` carries the new status, and the arrow function `(status) => move(ticket, status)` receives it.
The card does not change the ticket itself. The page decides what happens.

blocks.label: What you already know from Laravel
blocks.text: Props are like the variables you pass to a Blade component. Events are like Laravel events: one part announces something, another listens, and they do not know each other.

blocks.label: As in React
blocks.text: Props down works as in React. There, an event is a callback prop such as `onToggle`. In Vue you declare it as an event and call `emit('toggle')`.

blocks.label: Say it like this in an interview
blocks.text: Data flows down as props and messages flow up as events, so the parent always decides.

check.question: In `TicketRow.vue` someone clicks the checkbox. Which steps follow until the row looks different?
check.answer: The row sends `emit('toggle')`. The parent runs `toggle(ticket.id)` and changes `done`. The row then receives a new `done` prop and Vue redraws it.

deeper.text: A waiter (child) and a kitchen (parent). The kitchen hands the waiter a plate: those are the props. The waiter does not remake the dish, he takes it to the table.
If the guest says 'this is cold', the waiter calls it out to the kitchen: that is the event. The kitchen decides and sends out a new plate.

blocks.text: A composable is a plain function that bundles logic with state so several components can reuse it. By convention the name starts with `use`. Such a function usually returns refs.
Lifecycle hooks

items: `onMounted`: runs once the component is on the page. This is where you start things such as a timer.
`onBeforeUnmount`: runs just before the component goes away. This is where you clean up what you started.
A composable may call these hooks. They belong to the component that uses the composable.

blocks.text: In Sprintlab's own code
This is the whole file `resources/js/composables/useNow.ts`. It returns the current time as a ref that refreshes itself. Sprintlab uses it in `Dashboard.vue` and `Chat.vue`, among others.

blocks.caption: useNow.ts

items: `useNow(intervalMs = 60_000)` has a default of one minute. It returns a `Ref<number>`.
In `onMounted` it sets `now` and starts a timer that refreshes `now` every period.
In `onBeforeUnmount` it stops the timer. Without that, the timer would keep running after the component is gone.
A component uses it like this: `const now = useNow(60_000);` and then reads `now.value`.

blocks.text: Reacting to a change with watch
With `watch` you run code when a value changes. You use it for a side effect, such as saving or sending a request. For a derived value you use `computed`.

blocks.caption: Watch.vue

items: `watch(body, (newValue) => { ... })` runs every time `body` changes, and receives the new value.
This file also puts a timer straight into the component, as `useNow` does. That works, but if you repeat it in three components, you turn it into a composable.

blocks.label: What you already know from Laravel
blocks.text: A composable is like a service class you use in several controllers. The hooks are like model events such as `created` and `deleting`: fixed moments where you can hook in.

blocks.label: As in React
blocks.text: A composable is a custom hook. `onMounted` with `onBeforeUnmount` is like `useEffect` with a cleanup. `watch` is like `useEffect` with a dependency, but you name the source yourself.

blocks.label: Say it like this in an interview
blocks.text: A composable is a function that packages reusable stateful logic, and `useNow` starts a timer in `onMounted` and cleans it up in `onBeforeUnmount`.

check.question: What goes wrong if `useNow` does not stop the timer in `onBeforeUnmount`?
check.answer: The timer keeps running after the component is gone. It keeps updating the ref, and each time the component appears again an extra timer is added.

deeper.text: A composable is a toolbox you can put in any workshop. `useNow` is the box with an alarm clock in it.
`onMounted` is switching the alarm on when you open the workshop. `onBeforeUnmount` is switching it off when you lock the door. Forget that and it keeps ringing in an empty room.
`watch` is a doorbell: as soon as someone rings, you do something.

lessons.title: Vue with Laravel, and the older Options API

blocks.text: With Laravel there are two common ways to use Vue. You pick Inertia, or you build a separate Vue app that calls an API. On top of that, you will meet the Options API in older code.
Inertia: Laravel and Vue as one app
With Inertia, routes, controllers and login stay in Laravel. A controller returns not a Blade view but a Vue page with props. Sprintlab works this way.

blocks.caption: BoardController.php (shortened)

blocks.text: `Inertia::render('Board', [...])` picks the page `Board` and passes the array as props. In `resources/js/pages/Board.vue`, `defineProps` receives them.

blocks.caption: Board.vue

rows: Sends a PATCH request to Laravel without a full page load
Tracks form data, errors and a `processing` flag
Reloads props on an interval, without your own timer
Props that belong to every page, read with `usePage()`

blocks.text: Moving a ticket is a `router.patch`. `preserveScroll` and `preserveState` leave the page as it was.

blocks.caption: Board.vue

blocks.text: A form uses `useForm`, as `ChatComposer.vue` does. Errors from Laravel validation end up in `form.errors` by themselves.

blocks.caption: ChatComposer.vue

blocks.text: The board refreshes itself with `usePoll`, and reads a shared prop with `usePage()`.

blocks.caption: Board.vue

blocks.text: The shared props come from the middleware `app/Http/Middleware/HandleInertiaRequests.php`. Here are three of them, next to `auth` and `flash` among others.

blocks.caption: HandleInertiaRequests.php
blocks.code:
'sprint' => fn () => $this->sprintProps($request),
'unreadMessages' => fn () => $this->unreadMessages($request),
'sidebarOpen' => ! $request->hasCookie('sidebar_state') || $request->cookie('sidebar_state') === 'true',

blocks.text: A separate Vue app with an API
Here Laravel is only an API and Vue runs as its own project. Then you handle yourself what Inertia gives you.

rows: API requests, for example with axios

blocks.text: Vue Router is the official router for single-page Vue apps. Pinia is the store the Vue docs recommend for new apps. Axios is a separate library for sending HTTP requests.
Recognising the older Options API
Vue has two styles. The Options API organises code into options such as `data` and `methods`, and uses `this`. You saw the Composition API with `<script setup>` in this course.

blocks.caption: Options.vue
blocks.code:
<script>
export default {
    data() {
        return { count: 0 };
    },
    methods: {
        add() {
            this.count++;
        },
    },
};
</script>

<template>
    <button type="button" @click="add">Clicked: {{ count }}</button>
</template>

blocks.text: This is the same counter as `Counter.vue` from lesson 1. Both styles run on the same system. For full applications, the Vue docs recommend the Composition API with SFCs.

blocks.label: What you already know from Laravel
blocks.text: Inertia is the bridge that connects your controller straight to a Vue page: `Inertia::render` takes the place of `view()`. A separate app with an API is like a frontend that calls `routes/api.php`.

blocks.label: As in React
blocks.text: A separate Vue app with Vue Router and Pinia resembles a React app with React Router and a store. Inertia is closer to a server-driven app where the frontend is a Vue page.

blocks.label: Say it like this in an interview
blocks.text: `Inertia::render` connects a Laravel controller to a Vue page through props. A separate Vue app talks to Laravel only through an API.

check.question: What is the difference between Inertia and a separate Vue app with an API, in terms of routes and data?
check.answer: With Inertia, routes live in Laravel and data arrives as props from the controller. In a separate app, routes live in Vue Router and you fetch data through API requests.

deeper.text: Inertia is a restaurant with one kitchen. The kitchen (Laravel) and the dining room (Vue) belong together, and the waiter walks straight back and forth.
A separate app with an API is a takeaway with its own shop. The shop (Vue) orders by phone from the kitchen (the API), and you handle orders and the menu yourself.
The Options API is the same kitchen with an older recipe book: different handwriting, same dishes.

exercise.title: Build a task list in the Vue Playground
exercise.intro: You build a task list in the online Vue SFC Playground at play.vuejs.org. You do not need to install anything. It lets you practise `v-for`, `v-model`, `computed`, a form and a child component.
steps: Open play.vuejs.org and replace the contents of `App.vue` with the starter below.
Show the tasks in a `<ul>` with `v-for`. Give each `<li>` a `:key="task.id"` and show `{{ task.title }}`.
Put a checkbox in each row with `v-model="task.done"`. Give the title the class `done` when the task is done, with `:class="{ done: task.done }"`. Add a `<style scoped>` that strikes `.done` through.
Create a `computed` called `open` that counts how many tasks are not done yet. Show `Still to do: {{ open }}`.

Add a form with a `ref` called `newTitle`, an input with `v-model="newTitle"` and `@submit.prevent="add"`. In `add`, trim the spaces, stop on an empty title, and otherwise add a task and clear the field.
Add a **Remove** button to each task that calls a function `remove(task.id)`. In that function, keep all the other tasks.

Extra: create a child component `TaskRow.vue` (a new file in the Playground) with the props `title` and `done` and the events `toggle` and `remove`, like `TicketRow.vue` in lesson 4. Use it in `App.vue`.

solution.text: This is the complete solution, without the child component from the extra step. The code was compiled and run.

solution.caption: Todo.vue

items: `tasks` is a `ref` holding a list. `v-for` with `:key` shows them, and `v-model="task.done"` changes `done` directly.
`open` is a `computed`. It counts again as soon as a task is ticked, added or removed.
`@submit.prevent="add"` stops the page from reloading. `add` stops on an empty title and clears the field after adding.
`remove` builds a new list without the chosen task and assigns it to `tasks.value`.

solution.text: For the extra step, move the `<li>` into `TaskRow.vue`. Pass `title` and `done` as props and let the row send `toggle` and `remove`, just like `TicketRow.vue`.

quiz.question: What does `<script setup>` do for the template?
options: What you declare at the top level can be used directly in the template
It runs the code on the server instead of in the browser
It replaces the `<template>` block
It makes the component's CSS local
quiz.explanation: Top-level variables, functions and imports in `<script setup>` are available in the template without returning them.

quiz.question: In the script you read a ref as `count.value`. How do you show it in the template?
options: `{{ count.value }}`
`{{ ref(count) }}`
`{{ count }}`, Vue unwraps the value itself
`{{ $count }}`
quiz.explanation: Top-level refs are unwrapped automatically in the template, so you leave out `.value`.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of a `computed` over a function you call on every render?
options: A `computed` may also change data
The result is cached and only recalculated when a used value changes
A `computed` runs only on the server
A `computed` needs no `.value` in the script
quiz.explanation: A `computed` is cached. A method runs again on every render.

quiz.question: In `ChatComposer.vue`, `canSubmit` is a `computed`. What happens when the user types a character?
options: Nothing, `canSubmit` is calculated only once
You have to update `canSubmit` yourself in an event handler
The page reloads completely
`form.body` changes, so Vue recalculates `canSubmit` and the button follows
quiz.explanation: `canSubmit` uses `form.body`. When that changes, Vue recalculates it and the button adapts.

quiz.question: Why do you give `v-for` a `:key`?
options: So Vue recognises each element when the list changes, preferably with a unique `id`
Because `v-for` otherwise throws an error in the browser
To sort the list
To filter the list
quiz.explanation: The key gives each element a stable identity, so Vue reuses the right elements after a change.

quiz.question: What does `@submit.prevent="add"` do on a form?
options: It submits the form twice
It calls `add` and lets the browser submit the form itself
It calls `add` and stops the browser from submitting the form itself
It hides the form
quiz.explanation: The `.prevent` modifier calls `preventDefault()` on the event, so the page does not reload.

quiz.question: A child component wants a prop `done` to change. What does it do?
options: `props.done = true`, because props are plain variables
It sends an event, and the parent changes its own data
It reloads the page
It creates a new `computed` with the same name
quiz.explanation: Props are read-only. The child sends an event and the parent decides.

quiz.question: What does `defineEmits<{ toggle: [] }>()` declare?
options: A prop `toggle` of type array
An empty list of events
A `computed` called `toggle`
An event `toggle` that is sent without data
quiz.explanation: Between the brackets are the arguments that come with the event. Here there are none.

quiz.question: Why does `useNow` clean up the timer in `onBeforeUnmount`?
options: Because otherwise the timer keeps running after the component is gone
Because otherwise `onMounted` cannot start the timer
Because otherwise a `ref` is not reactive
Because otherwise Vue runs the timer on the server
quiz.explanation: What you start in `onMounted` must be cleaned up when the component goes away.

quiz.question: When do you pick `watch` and when `computed`?
options: `watch` to derive a value, `computed` for side effects
`watch` for a side effect on a change, `computed` for a derived value
They do the same thing, it makes no difference
`watch` only in templates, `computed` only in scripts
quiz.explanation: `computed` is for calculating a value. `watch` is for doing something, such as saving, when something changes.

quiz.question: What does `Inertia::render('Board', [...])` do in a controller?
options: It returns a JSON API response without Vue
It compiles `Board.vue` to HTML on the server and sends only HTML
It creates a Vue Router route
It picks the Vue page `Board` and passes the array as props
quiz.explanation: The name points to the page component and the array becomes its props.

quiz.question: You see `data() { return { count: 0 } }` and `this.count++`. What is the Composition API equivalent?
options: `const count = ref(0)` and `count.value++`
`const count = computed(0)` and `count++`
`defineProps({ count: 0 })` and `props.count++`
`watch(count, 0)` and `count.value = 1`
quiz.explanation: `data()` becomes a `ref`, and `this.count` becomes `count.value` in the script.
